p: The KJV's "all these things must come to pass" adds "all."

p: The KJV adds "pestilences." The two Greek words look almost alike.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (01, 300s, first hand), Vaticanus (B, 300s), Bezae (D, 400s), some Old Latin manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
Codex Ephraemi (C, 400s), most later manuscripts, the Syriac and Coptic versions; Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV); the Vulgate has the words in the order 'pestilences and famines'

why: The oldest manuscripts lack "plagues," and Luke 21:11 has both words, so scribes may have added it from Luke. On the other side, limoi and loimoi differ by one letter, and Tischendorf thought a scribe's eye skipped from one to the other. The Plain English Translation follows the modern editions, but the case is close.

a: The angels of heaven do not know, and the Son does not know. Only the Father knows.
p: The oldest manuscripts say even the Son does not know. Many others, including Washingtonianus (W, 400s), leave this out.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (01, 300s, first hand), Vaticanus (B, 300s), Bezae (D, 400s), Θ (800s) and family 13, as the NA28/UBS5 apparatus reports; most Old Latin manuscripts, the Palestinian Syriac, the Armenian and Ethiopic versions; Irenaeus (in Latin), Origen's commentary (in Latin), Chrysostom, Hilary; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.orig: οὐδὲ οἱ ἄγγελοι τῶν οὐρανῶν οὐδὲ ὁ υἱός, εἰ μὴ ὁ πατὴρ μόνος
readings.en: not the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father alone
readings.plain: The angels of heaven do not know, and the Son does not know. Only the Father knows.

readings.w: A corrector of Sinaiticus, Codex Regius (L), Washingtonianus (W, 400s), family 1, 33 and most later manuscripts, as the NA28/UBS5 apparatus reports; the Vulgate, the Peshitta and other Syriac versions (not the Palestinian Syriac), the Coptic; Basil; Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: οὐδὲ οἱ ἄγγελοι τῶν οὐρανῶν, εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ μου μόνος
readings.en: not the angels of heaven, but my Father alone
readings.plain: The angels of heaven do not know. Only my Father knows.

why: The words have very early and widespread support, and it is easy to see why scribes would drop them: they seemed to make the Son less than the Father. It is hard to see why anyone would add them. The word "alone" also fits best if the Son has just been named. Mark 13:32 has "nor the Son" in every manuscript.
b: This is one of the clearest cases where a theological worry shaped the text. Jerome noted that some Latin copies had "nor the Son" while the Greek copies of Origen and Pierius did not. The two Origen witnesses are not a contradiction: the Latin translation of Origen's commentary reads the words, while Jerome reports Greek copies associated with Origen that lacked them. Ambrose suspected the words had been added by heretics. Basil took Matthew's text as lacking them. The Byzantine text also reads "my Father," which Matthew often says. See the note on this verse.

readings.plain: to meet the groom and the bride

why: The Greek evidence is overwhelming. The addition probably came from a custom in which the groom brought his bride home, or from a wish to give the bride a place in the story. The Harclean Syriac itself notes in its margin that the words are not in all copies.
b: Some scholars think the shorter text shows the church reading the groom as Christ, whose bride is the church itself, so a second bride would confuse the picture.
